title: Redwood Data Retention Demo - Harbor Payments
summary: Redwood walked Harbor Payments through the data handling and retention controls available in the API, Console, and Optimize tooling. Primary focus was on logging redaction, PII detection/auto-redaction, request storage toggles (per-org, per-api-key, per-route), audit logs, and KMS-backed encryption for private deployments. Harbor's security team asked about retention windows, ability to disable request storage for PCI-scope flows, and integration with their existing KMS and SIEM. Redwood committed to sharing SOC2 artifacts, a short runbook for KMS setup in Private, and a sample config for per-route storage toggles and redaction rules.
next_steps: Ava to send SOC2 + ISO docs and security whitepaper by 2026-04-30
Ravi to share sample per-route retention config and demo recording by 2026-05-01

transcript:
Meeting header: 2026-04-28 15:00 UTC | Duration: ~45m | Attendees: Ava Martinez (Redwood AE), Ravi Patel (Redwood SE), Ellen Cho (Product), Maya Chen (Harbor - Head of Security), Liam O'Connor (Harbor - CTO), Sofia Alvarez (Harbor - Platform Eng), Devon Park (Harbor - Compliance)

[00:00] Ava: hey everyone, thanks for joining, i'm ava from redwood, i'll kick us off and ravi will do the demo, um quick agenda — show the console controls for data retention, the api toggles, and a bit on optimize for how you can keep quality monitoring without holding raw customer PII.
[00:15] Liam: great, thanks ava. quick note, we really are looking at this from a pci-scope perspective, so anything that touches cardholder data, we need to make sure it's never stored by a third party.
[00:25] Maya: yep and we also want to understand the audit trail — who changes retention settings, and how to forward logs to our SIEM.
[00:32] Ava: absolutely, that's exactly what we'll cover. ravi over to you.
[00:36] Ravi: cool thanks. so first, console view — i'll share my screen, uh if you go to settings -> data handling, you can see org-level defaults for request storage: 30 days, 90 days, 1 year, or disabled. you can override that at api-key level or route level. here's a sample route override for /payments/authorize where we set storage = disabled. so for pci flows you can toggle off storage entirely, which means the platform will not persist request bodies beyond ephemeral processing.
[01:05] Ravi: (small pause) note there's streaming telemetry that still records token counts and latency metrics but not the full request payload when storage is disabled.
[01:15] Sofia: how's that implemented — is it a flag on the request or per-key policy?
[01:19] Ravi: it's policy based. when the request comes in the routing layer evaluates policy ordered by: route override, api-key policy, org default. policy is enforced by the ingestion layer, so we short-circuit persistence if storage=false. in private deployments the same control exists but data never leaves your VPC unless you opt into the hosted analytics pipeline.
[01:38] Maya: and about redaction — can you auto-detect pii fields inside complex json? we have nested payloads.
[01:43] Ravi: yes — we have a PII detection policy that runs regex and ML-based detectors, you can enable auto-redact where matched spans are replaced with {REDACTED} before any persistence. we also support token-level hashing and deterministic tokenization if you need referential mapping without storing original values.
[02:02] Liam: hmm, regex plus ml — what about false positives/negatives, we need to be able to review and tune rules.
[02:08] Ravi: good question. the console has a ruleset editor, you can preview rules against sample payloads in the UI. we'll show that — here's a sample rule that matches card numbers and straps on expiry date, and you can set severity or make it a blocking rule so requests with detected PANs are rejected or routed to a manual-review queue rather than persisted.
[02:30] Devon: manual-review queue — does that still store the payload? we can't have PANs in logs.
[02:34] Ravi: in blocking mode the request is not persisted; we surface metadata like request id and timestamp to your audit log but not the payload. if you opt for manual review you can set a strict retention policy on that queue or configure it to stream to a customer-managed S3 bucket in your account with KMS encryption.
[02:50] Maya: ok that helps. on encryption — for private deployments we want KMS/HSM integration with key rotation. what's supported?
[02:58] Ellen: i'll take that — in Private we support customer-managed KMS via the cloud providers' KMS or an HSM integration. keys are used for at-rest encryption of persisted requests and for envelope encryption of smaller secrets. we also support bringing-your-own-KMS for the hosted dedicated tenants where you manage the key in your cloud provider and we store only encrypted blobs.
[03:15] Liam: and how are audit logs handled? we need a tamper-evident trail and ability to forward to Splunk or Datadog.
[03:22] Ravi: audit logs capture config changes, who changed them (SSO user mapping), API-key creates/rotates, and retention toggles. logs can be pushed via syslog, or forwarded to your SIEM via a secure connector — we also offer an immutable audit export (weekly) for compliance reviews.
[03:38] Maya: there's sometimes transcription weirdness — forgive me — does SSO map to internal user ids? we need RBAC.
[03:44] Ava: yes we support SAML SSO with SCIM provisioning, and roles map down to RBAC in the console. change events include the principal id, so you get the who/when in the audit trail.
[03:55] Liam: what's the retention enforcement model for retention windows vs legal hold? say legal gets a hold on a customer transaction — can we override retention?
[04:02] Ravi: legal hold is supported as a higher-priority flag. legal hold can pin specific request ids or customer ids and prevents automatic deletion until explicitly released. that action is captured in the audit log and requires an elevated role to apply.
[04:14] Sofia: cool. show us the API flow — how we'd toggle storage per-request if we wanted to?
[04:19] Ravi: two options — per-request header (x-redwood-store: disable) if your client can set it, and server-side policy via api keys or route config. per-request header is honored only if the api-key policy allows it, so you can't override org policy from a client.
[04:32] Maya: are there rate-limit or cost implications if we disable persistence but still do quality monitoring?
[04:36] Ravi: disabling persistence reduces storage costs but you lose the ability to replay requests for evals. Redwood Optimize provides sampled evaluations: you can keep sampling enabled but apply redaction hooks before persistence, or send hashed tokens. there's also a live-token-aggregation mode that keeps aggregate metrics for quality without storing raw text.
[04:56] Liam: so Optimize can compute eval metrics without the raw PII? what's the sampling approach?
[05:01] Ravi: yes — we do deterministic sampling by request id, you can pick 0.1% up to 100%. sampled requests can be routed to a secure bucket with customer KMS, or redacted before storage. the Optimize pipeline supports differential privacy style noise if you want further guarantees, although that's an advanced option.
[05:20] Maya: we'll want to see a config that sets sampling to 1% but always disables storage for pci routes.
[05:25] Ava: we'll include a sample policy for that.
[05:28] Ravi: moving on to console demo — here's the rule editor, you can add detectors: regex (fast), ML (fuzzy), or custom webhook where you call your own PII service. the editor shows preview matches and a confidence score. note: transcription sometimes shows the model names wrong — it's the ml-detector shipping with the platform, we can label it for you.
[05:50] (screen shared, typing sounds)
[06:05] Ravi: previewing sample payload... oh, small transcription glitch, the preview text looks a bit off — but you can see the detector matching "card_number": "4111..." and we replace it client-side with ****REDACTED**** for persistence.
[06:18] Sofia: can we maintain a reversible token in our own keyspace so we can re-link if needed?
[06:22] Ravi: yes that's where deterministic hashing or customer-side tokenization comes in. you can supply a hash salt stored in your KMS so redwood sees hashed identifiers but cannot revert them. alternative is to have the tokenization happen in your sidecar before it hits Redwood.
[06:36] Liam: how does this affect latency? we need sub-200ms 95th for auth calls.
[06:41] Ravi: the PII detection is optimized for short-circuiting; regex detectors run inline and are microseconds, ML detectors can be async unless you enable blocking mode. for blocking/per-route you can choose synchronous detection (adds a small tail, typically 10-30ms) or asynchronous (no added latency, detection happens post-response and affects persistence only).
[07:05] Maya: synchronous is risky for auth; we'll probably want async with strict redaction before persistence.
[07:11] Ravi: that pattern is common — inline metrics retained, payload processed off the main path and redacted before hitting storage.
[07:17] Devon: for compliance we need proofs of deletion. does Redwood give deletion receipts?
[07:22] Ravi: yes, deletions generate a signed deletion receipt with timestamp and request id. receipts are accessible via the API and are also written to the audit log. for private deployments receipts can be written to your S3 and signed with your KMS.
[07:36] Sofia: show us the API example to request deletion.
[07:39] Ravi: sure — there's an admin endpoint DELETE /v1/requests/{id} with admin scope. the response includes receipt_id and deletion_timestamp. we'll share curl samples after the call.
[07:50] Liam: curious about data residency — we have eu customers, do you have region controls for where requests are persisted?
[07:55] Ava: yes, per-tenant region control. for hosted we have eu and na regions; Dedicated you can choose the region and in Private it's entirely customer-managed.
[08:05] Maya: on the forwarding to SIEM, can we redact or hash fields in the forwarded logs?
[08:10] Ravi: yes the log-forwarding pipeline supports transformation rules — you can specify field-level redaction or hash strategies before forwarding. it's useful for e.g., sending events to datadog without PII.
[08:20] Liam: any gotchas with long-term metrics retention vs payload retention?
[08:24] Ravi: token/metric retention and raw payload retention are decoupled. metrics (counts, latency histograms) are stored longer for billing/analytics, but they don't contain payload. raw payloads adhere to the retention window you configured.
[08:35] Liam: ok good. do you support per-tenant service accounts for programmatic changes so we can automate retention changes?
[08:40] Ellen: yes service accounts with scoped tokens, and all changes are audited. you can rotate keys via the API.
[08:46] Maya: about PII detection accuracy — can we run our own detector inside the pipeline?
[08:50] Ravi: yep, custom webhook detectors let you call out to your own service; we also have a local sidecar that can run your models in Private. performance depends on your model.
[08:59] Liam: any examples of customers using the manual-review queue for low-volume high-sensitivity flows?
[09:04] Ravi: yes banks often route chargeback appeals to manual-review with strict retention; those queues are typically mapped to a customer-managed bucket and have additional access controls.
[09:12] (short pause)
[09:20] Ravi: i'll demo the per-route policy JSON — here is a snippet: {"route":"/payments/authorize","storage":"disabled","pii_detection":{"mode":"auto-redact","detectors":["regex_cards","ml_name"]},"sampling":{"optimize":0.01}} — (note: transcription may mangle some braces).
[09:38] Maya: can you make that downloadable from the console?
[09:40] Ravi: yes you can export/import policies as JSON.
[09:44] Liam: on policy precedence — route override > api-key > org default, correct?
[09:48] Ravi: correct.
[09:50] Maya: what about rollbacks — if someone accidentally changes retention?
[09:54] Ellen: the console supports canary changes and you can require two-person approval for retention updates. also every change is versioned and you can rollback via the UI or API.
[10:05] Devon: what about data subject requests? we need to support right-to-erasure workflows.
[10:10] Ravi: Redwood exposes user-level delete APIs and bulk deletion tools for DSARs. bulk deletions can be scoped by customer id or timeframe. deletions generate receipts and are auditable.
[10:21] Maya: ok that's the functionality. do you do retention reporting — like weekly exports of stored request counts and pending legal-holds?
[10:28] Ava: yes we can schedule retention reports and include counts, sizes, and outstanding holds. we'll show sample reports in the follow-up.
[10:34] (screen: demo continues, showing sample reports)
[11:00] Ravi: quick note on mis-transcriptions — the detector name is "pii-ml-v2" in our docs, sometimes the speech-to-text renders as "pie ml v two" in the transcript, sorry about that.
[11:08] Liam: haha noted.
[11:12] Maya: what's the process for the POC — if we want to prove we can avoid persisting pan data?
[11:17] Ava: typical POC: we spin up a dedicated tenant or private trial, configure route-level storage disabled for pci endpoints, run a workload for 48-72 hours, you give us sample payloads and we run the detectors, then we'll generate a deletion/retention report and show receipts for any deleted items.
[11:33] Liam: and cost model for that dedicated trial?
[11:36] Ava: we usually provide a time-boxed trial; cost depends on the reserved capacity for throughput. we'll include pricing options in the follow-up.
[11:44] Maya: any security docs we can share today?
[11:47] Ava: i'll drop SOC2, ISO, penetration test summary and the redwood security whitepaper after the call.
[11:53] Ravi: lastly, about streaming responses — streaming doesn't change storage unless you explicitly turn on persistence. streaming sessions produce ephemeral tokens that are not stored unless you opt-in.
[12:05] Devon: fine.
[12:08] (silence, then wrap)
[12:12] Ava: ok quick recap: we'll send security artifacts, sample per-route policy, demo recording, and a suggested POC plan. harbor will share sample payloads and confirm the POC dates. any final q's?
[12:25] Liam: none here, thanks.
[12:28] Maya: thanks all.
[12:30] Ava: thanks everyone, we'll follow up.

End of transcript.

Notes on transcription quality: medium — a few proper nouns and code snippets were mangled by the auto-transcriber; timestamps approximate.
